claims.text: Conventionally additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components typically exhibit large thermal gradients.
Conventionally additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components typically exhibit residual stresses, porosity, and microstructural irregularities.
An in-situ laser re-melting step should be applied immediately after deposition of each layer.
Using lower laser power and adjusted scanning speed relative to primary melting enables partial re-melting and reflow.
Properly controlled partial re-melting avoids excessive grain growth.
Layer-by-layer laser re-melting produces a more uniform and refined grain structure.
Layer-by-layer laser re-melting decreases porosity.
Layer-by-layer laser re-melting diminishes residual-stress concentrations.
The proposed structural changes result from improved melt-pool fusion and controlled solidification.
Re-melting and re-solidification of each fresh layer occur under milder thermal gradients than conventional processing.
Milder thermal gradients reduce rapid thermal contraction and residual stress.
Reduced rapid thermal contraction minimizes dimensional distortion.
In-situ laser re-melting heals microscopic voids and micro-cracks.
Healing voids and micro-cracks creates a more mechanically coherent structure.
Relative to conventional additive manufacturing, in-situ layer re-melting improves dimensional precision.
Relative to conventional additive manufacturing, in-situ layer re-melting increases yield strength.
Relative to conventional additive manufacturing, in-situ layer re-melting increases fatigue resistance.
Relative to conventional additive manufacturing, in-situ layer re-melting lowers the density of fabrication-induced defects.
The benefits require an optimal processing window that avoids over-melting, grain coarsening, and new defect formation.
The intervention applies primarily to high-entropy-alloy systems prone to thermal-stress-induced imperfections.
